# Top 5 posts from r/MovieSuggestions day

## 1. Looking for movies where people are invited/go somewhere and slowly realize something is wrong (Thrillers)

**Score:** 75
**Body:** I’m looking for thrillers where the main character is invited to somoones house, a vacation, a dinner, a remote place, etc and everything initially seems relatively normal, but they slowly start realizing that something is very wrong.



Movies like Get Out, Speak No Evil, A cure for wellness, Skeleton Key and The Visit are exactly the kind of thing I’m looking for.



I really like that uncomfortable feeling where the hosts are acting strange, but the characters aren’t sure whether they’re actually in danger or just being paranoid

### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. The Invitation (2015)

The Menu (2022)
  - The Invitation is *so good*.
2. The Green Room is as good as this genre gets
3. The Others - A family lives in a darkened mansion with a rare illness-- extreme sensitivity to sunlight. Awesome movie. Don't look up anything about it.
4. Midsommar
5. I also vote for The Menu
6. Barbarian
7. Ex Machina  also the tv series DEVS
8. A Perfect getaway (2009)
9. Vivarium might fit the bill 

## 2. Red Rooms is really good.

**Score:** 53
**Body:** It's not an action movie. It's not a horror movie, in the traditional sense. But it's really interesting and well done, if you are into this kind of thing. Although, I recommend watching it without reading anything about it, even though it pretty messed up so some people won't be into it at all. I'm not sure I've seen anything like it. 

### Top 6 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. It's pretty amazing how stomach churning this movie is at some points without actually showing any violence at all.
You only hear bits and pieces and see the reactions the videomaterial has on the people in the courtroom, but you yourself as a viewer never actually see anything.

It's an awesome movie and kind of a hidden gem, you rarely see people bringing it up even though IMO it's one of the best horror adjacent movies of the last couple of years.
  - Agreed; loved the fandom / dark use of tech themes. Tone-wise it reminded me of Thesis, another slightly more horror entrenched, gem
    - Never heard about Thesis, definitely gonna watch it now though. Thanks :)
  - I'm certain that scene just outside the courtroom door where you can only hear the video is inspired by a real-life video taken outside the courtroom door at the trial of the Toolbox Killers, Lawrence Bittaker and Roy Norris, when they played the recording they made of the torture-murder of Shirley Ledford. It's on youtube.
  - That restraint honestly made it way more disturbing, your imagination fills in everything they refuse to show
2. one of those movies that leaves you staring at a blank screen during the credits try to process what you just watched. absolute masterpiece, but definitely not for everyone
3. The filmmaker and leading actresses did an AMA a couple years ago that was insightful: [https://www.reddit.com/r/movies/comments/1fobizk/hello\_rmovies\_we\_are\_pascal\_plante\_juliette/](https://www.reddit.com/r/movies/comments/1fobizk/hello_rmovies_we_are_pascal_plante_juliette/)
4. Yeah its great.

Try kill list 
5. It wasn’t really my thing but I’m glad I saw it. Horror should keep pushing the boundary of art and fear. 

## 3. Best westerns for a newbie to the genre?

**Score:** 27
**Body:** I'm a big fan of the space western Trigun, and in general I also love the western aesthetic and culture. I have seen maybe half of A Fistful of Dollars, and I've watched maybe a quarter of an episode of Bonanza.

I am a big fan of country/western music, especially the kind that narrates stories and are about Cowboys or western life. Specifically, I love Marty Robbins' Gunfighter Ballads.

With this in mind, I want to start watching western movies but I don't know where to begin. What are some good/quintessential ones to start with?

### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. True Grit
  - Yes, the 2010 one!
2. A few dollars more

The Good, The Bad and the Ugly

Once Upon a time in the West

Tombstone

Young Guns one and two 
3. High Noon (1952)

The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance (1962)

Monte Walsh (1970)

The Ox-Bow Incident (1943)

Red River (1948)

Rio Bravo (1959)

The Searchers (1956)

Shane (1953)

Stagecoach (1939)
4. Tombstone

High Plaines Drifter

The Magnificent Seven 1960
5. Tombstone is the absolute best starting point for a newcomer. 

Val Kilmer steals every scene he's in. It hits all the classic cowboy tropes without feeling slow or dated. After that, check out The Good, the Bad and the Ugly.
6. Silverado 
7. Lonesome Dove. All of it. In one sitting
8. Delve into some Peckinpah! Very violent films but they're fantastic. 

The Wild Bunch (1969) and Pat Garrett and Billy the Kid (1973) are probably his two best westerns to start with.
9. Unforgiven (1992)

## 4. [SUGGESTING] Go see The End of Oak Street (2026)

**Score:** 26
**Body:** Just saw *The End of Oak Street* (2026). If you’re on the fence, go see it. I went in with no expectations and had a blast.

It’s refreshing to see an original, simple story that doesn’t over-explain itself. It’s funny, scary, charming, campy, and surprisingly emotional, with a great cast led by Anne Hathaway and Ewan McGregor.

Best of all, the dinosaurs are actually scary again.This is the kind of grounded "creature feature" I wish Jurassic Park had continued making.

Not perfect, but I genuinely felt like a kid again and it is the most fun I have had at the movies in a LONG time. Solid 8.5/10.

### Top 8 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Agreed! The 80s nostalgia is one thing that doesn’t get mentioned. I love the way that the dinos were done, they didn’t look familiar at all like we have got used to in Jurassic Park and World Series. 

I could pick countless holes in the movie, but it was solid entertainment, in my current top 5 of the year so far!
  - Exactly, the dinos actually feeling unfamiliar again was such a refreshing change from the usual Jurassic look
2. I'll backup this suggestion.

These middle of the road blockbusters have been sorely missed. Don't go in expecting some big epic. Go in expecting a movie thats just trying to have fun with a concept, yet still knows how to create a good story through its characters. Its very aware of its genre yet never bridges too far into satire. It has a heart at its core, but it also never takes itself too seriously. Its humor never truly undercuts the impending danger. It really is just a well-balanced fun summer blockbuster.
3. I love how much love this movie is getting 🍾
4. I took my teens to see it and we really enjoyed it! 
5. It's like the most 6.5/10 film I've seen in a while. It's fun and entertaining, with a good cast and performances, but outside of a few moments it never firmly crosses over from being good into great. 

With how much of a love letter it is to 80s and 90s summer release, family oriented action-adventure films, it ended up being the most, and best, Spielberg-like film I've seen this year, and that includes having watched Disclosure Day, an actual Spielberg film. 
  - This is a fair take. It was all over the place with its tone not in a good way, and some of it was just dumb, but I can’t deny that once the action got going it was fun &entertaining . Was laughing at the film more than I was laughing with it, but that still counts. 

And agree with the sentiment of op and others that are happy to see an original movie like this get made and do well
6. I'm excited to see it at a Drive-In next weekend. When I saw this was coming out, the thing that stood out was that its not a sequel, not remake, not a superhero, not animated...I don't care if it gets compared to Jurassic Park, I hope studios will take more risks creating  "tweaked" stories comparable to tried and true concepts.
7. I was unsure how David Robert Mitchell's writing and directing would work for this and it was perfect. I had so much fun. Will definitely re-watch often. An instant classic in my opinion. 
8. Yeah, this was a pretty good change of pace from the Jurassic World series and its perpetually aura farming dinosaurs. I liked that it didn’t dive too deep into the >!time travel/portal aspect as well!< and kept it mostly focused on the family. >!I was pretty shocked when the dad died though, definitely thought they would all either make it through unscathed or just adapt to a new prehistoric life somehow by the end.!<

## 5. Movies for someone who is struggling to love life.

**Score:** 22
**Body:** I’ve been depressed essentially my whole life, but for the most part, I’ve still been able to find the pleasure in living, if only for the moments of joy in between the pain. However, I’ve reached the point where I’m left asking “what’s the point?” Even when I’m doing something subjectively fun, I’m left thinking “what purpose is this really serving?” Is there a movie that tackles similar themes and will help me rediscover my love for life?

### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Napoleon Dynamite 
2. The Secret Life of Walter Mitty, especially if you feel stuck
3. School of Rock 
4. The Sound of Metal  
Groundhog Day  
Good Will Hunting 
5. A beautiful life 1997

Watch it with subs as original is in italian but you'll thank me later.
6. I don’t have a long list of movie recs. I will say that when I was struggling before I connected with Castaway. 

I’m kind of right there with you. Not a movie but on Facebook Instagram I read Humans of New York. For podcasts, I listen to Storycorps. 
7. City Slickers is about exactly that. I think it’ll speak to where you’re at on a profound level. Parenthood is wonderful, too.
8. perfect days

i can’t stress enough how this will change your perspective
9. Little Miss Sunshine
10. Singing’ In The Rain; it’s a tonic to make you feel good.

## 1. Hot Take: I Miss Kang.

**Score:** 1065
**Body:** Kang..

What happened to him?

The guy went from being the objectively most powerful risk for the multiverse then he suddenly became an afterthought and often coupled with absolute ridicule due to his only real portrayal in Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania.

(I’ll address the third Antman 3 as “Q” from now now on.)

Q had the most ridiculous experience and we have to never ignore how bad Q hurted Kang.

Before the allegations, Kang is the guy who should have screwed Michelle Pfeiffer, he felt like this buffed ass fake muscular extremely sophisticated coming-from-the-future absolute madman.

He has like an exponential power level of intellect compared to Einstein.

He’s has sort of Einstein AND Schrödinger level of scientific knowledge : to the infinite power!

He was also “He Who Remains” or whatever that BS in Loki is.  
I never really liked Loki as much as I felt I was gonna like it.

I didn’t even watch Loki Season 3 yet but I know Loki becomes “in the place of” He Who Remains. Or wait… isn’t Sylvie the Hot Female Loki the one who killed him? What even happened to her? She was Hot tho.

But lets go back to Kang.

He was also in Creed 3. We were supposed to love Jonathan Majors like we are always supposed to love the Star Power of Zendaya. He was the MBJ twin bestie. I wasnt against that.

But honestly? I always felt Kang.. and Jonathan Majors’ “suddern buffed up status of Star Power” never really convincing.

Kang LACKED aura because he was written in a way that has inherent aura. Not “acquiring the aura”.

Thanos acquired his aura through buildup. He was always the “finish line of villains’ power”.

Kang feels ridiculously powerful compares to Thanos to the point Thanos is currently somewhat “ridiculed” or “underrated” by comparison.

Thanos will always be the best villain Marvel created. I hated what they did to him in that animated show where a stupidly ridiculously Overpowered version of Ultron from a different universe dissects him in half like some Mortal Kombat Fatality.

Screw you.

Kang is a badly written villain.

Ant-Man (ironically) Defeated him.  
Ant-Man who is always ridiculed for being that other random superhero.. ACTUALLY objectively defeated Kang.

The billions of Kang versions in the multiverse can possibly always be defeated by an Ant-Man.

We know they will never explore this. Kang is no more. Not even dead. Not even respected for his history like the Deadpool 2 villain (Cable).

Kang failed because he was always never gonna be taken as seriously as Thanos.

Kang sounded fake. Forced. Manufactured. Written poorly. Buffed for nothing. An Ant-Man villain. One that didnt even have enough courage to go for Michelle Pfeiffer even tho they lived together alone for ages or some S. and she banged that old comedian (established in the same movie).

Lemme put this right here and you know it’s a fact:

Kang was just Jonathan Majors with different clothes.

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. Devil wears Prada 2: are we supposed to care about the characters?

**Score:** 87
**Body:** I remember when I saw the first Devil Wear Prada, even though I wasn't particularly interested in the world of fashion and the like, I was quite entertained. The audience could identify with the protagonist, the classic fish out of water, and of course Meryl Streep was a delight to watch.

But while watching the sequel, I realized something. I couldn't care less what happened to the characters. Sure, Anne Hathaway loses her job as a journalist but quickly finds another. But what about Miranda? Are we really supposed to root for a misanthropic, rich woman in her seventies whether she keeps her job or not? Whether the magazine stays open or closed? Sure, theoretically it can be disappointing if the people who work there lose their jobs, but in the film this particular aspect is never treated seriously.

At the end, there are all the twists and turns, and I realized that I simply couldn't care less. The magazine is sold, or isn't sold, so? The other "emotional" part of the film is when Stanley Tucci's character is "allowed" to give the opening speech at the fashion show. I watched the scene and it was clearly presented as a great climactic moment (the character's emotion, the music, the cinematography), but I thought, "These people make more money than I'll ever see in my life, and should I be moved by that?"

As I said, I'm not the best audience for this film, but I wondered: was the intent really to make us somehow root for these characters, or maybe I misunderstood and are we supposed to consider them all horrible people with no redeeming qualities?

Because in the first case, the film simply failed. In the second, well, not only did it escape me, but I was also bored.

So I was asking your opinion: does the film somehow try to make us sympathize with the characters and root for them and I didn't get it, or should we start from the assumption that they are all shallow people and we should, I don't know, feel better because money doesn't buy happiness or something?

### Top 6 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. it's not a movie. it's a cash grab where the filmmakers barely read the script to judge if it made any sense.

people like Miranda in the first movie cuz she's great at her job - she's just bitchy executing it. here, she's still bitchy but doesn't seem to be any good at being the boss editor. the triggering crisis is *Runway* publishes a positive story about a fashion brand that uses sweatshops. it got published during Miranda's watch! the publisher hires Andy back to get some good press -behind Miranda's back - so Miranda makes a big show of firing the features editor by phone so that Andy can take over. The features editor is the one responsible for the sweatshop crisis; she should've been fired anyway.

you mention Nigel getting to make the opening speech at the fashion show as an emotional moment. actually, he doesn't get to make a speech. the movie cuts away from him just as he starts. this is the crowning moment of Miranda's dedicated, long-suffering right-hand man who is finally getting what he's always wanted. and the movie has no time for it.

this movie resolves the the issue of a billionaire buying the magazine for ulterior motives by...having another billionaire buy it from the first billionaire. yeah, it's that stoopid.

here's the worst: Emily Blunt's character turns out to be the surprise villain of the movie. but it's still Emily Blunt so she shows up again at the end cuz Andy meets her for lunch and they talk it out without any hint of animosity. bitch, she stabbed up in the back and tried to steal the magazine. u really gonna break bread with her?!?
  - >here's the worst: Emily Blunt's character turns out to be the surprise villain of the movie. but it's still Emily Blunt so she shows up again at the end cuz Andy meets her for lunch and they talk it out without any hint of animosity. bitch, she stabbed up in the back and tried to steal the magazine. u really gonna break bread with her?!?

Thanks. I thought I was stupid and missing something! "Uh, why are you chatting sweetly with this filthy traitor?"
    - There are huge gaps in the narrative where things obviously got cut for time. Like the boyfriend character basically existed for one scene where Andy treats him like shit and then later on it's like nothing happened. Or the bit where Stanley Tucci tells Andy that whatever she does she cannot get a stain on her dress, and then she does and there's zero consequence to it, the film just forgets that it had set up that conflict.
      - Wow that's lazy
2. We're obviously "supposed" to, but we don't. TDWP2 is a classic example of sequelitis and almost entirely fails to justify its own existence. I do think it's interesting that they considered the current media landscape and used that to talk about the impact of big tech and venture capital on traditional media, but the actual film is really boring and they don't actually do anything with those ideas.

In my opinion, the biggest mistake _was_ the characters. The first film is all about Andy's journey, learning to be less judgemental while also navigating the ethical ramifications of the cutthroat industry she found herself, all while her life moves in a different direction from everyone she cares about. In the sequel, no-one really learns or navigates anything, at the end of the film everyone is the same character they started with very little personal conflict or growth and it sucks.

If _I_ were making the film, I would probably make Andy "the devil". I would massively diminish Miranda's role if not cut it entirely (she'd probably have to stay for the marketing of course). Then that gives Andy an obvious space for her to grow into, as well as makes room for another Andy-esque junior character to centre the film around.

But really they just shouldn't have made it. The first film is the kind of film that was perfect by accident and it's hard to capture that lightning in a bottle again
  - Right, a HUGE part of the story of the original was that Miranda was becoming “outdated” as a type of leader. Too expensive, too demanding, too old.

Now she’s way too old, likely just as expensive, and the only thing that’s changed is she can’t throw coats anymore.

It felt so off. I think anyone with her gravitas would’ve pivoted to a “creative consultant” or something over whatever happened to her. Or she would’ve been pushed out a decade before the film.
3. I agree with your comments about the film. I felt the same way. It’s hard to care about wealthy people losing their jobs. Miranda probably made more money every year than most people see in a lifetime of working. If she’s broke after losing her job, that’s her own fault. 

The movie does accidentally show how pretentious and out of touch rich people are compared to regular people. Asking us to give a shit about them was a bit much. The movie also shows a narcissist and her enablers. We see Miranda in full force, acting entitled, ungrateful, selfish, using everyone around her. However, films portray men like her all the time and people love them. 

I think some in Hollywood think that the masses believe or want to believe that money is the happily ever after. It’s condescending and the movie actually shows us that the wealthy are flawed and shouldn’t be idolized. Often they are only wealthy due to luck. Their talent and business sense is negotiable. 
  - >I agree with your comments about the film. I felt the same way. It’s hard to care about wealthy people losing their jobs. Miranda probably made more money every year than most people see in a lifetime of working. If she’s broke after losing her job, that’s her own fault.

Then there is a detail that is immediately set aside in the film. Hanna Hatway's character returns to work at the magazine because Miranda is under fire for publishing a puff piece about a brand that uses sweatshop labor.

Now I don't know, are we supposed to believe it's a trifle? A venial sin in the grand scheme of things? Miranda never shows any regret for what she's done. Should I root for someone like that?
4. To me it seemed the film was art imitating life. Remember the rumor that Jeff Bezos was buying Vogue for his wife, Lauren Sanchez? Emily's evil rich tech bro boyfriend and his equally rich ex-wife who actually cares about stuff are obviously inspired by Jeff and his ex wife Mackenzie.   

5. The first film made us understand that it’s not just clothes. The second film is just the clothes with the folks wearing them mannequins (albeit with less personality than the average mannequin)

## 2. The Odyssey Belongs to All of Us

**Score:** 74
**Body:** -A great read by a classic philosophy professor about the academic response to The Odyssey.

https://dissentmagazine.org/online_articles/christopher-nolan-odyssey-review/

In particular this passage 
>It takes seriously both what the text is doing and how it has been read since. It’s the sort of adaptation that paves the way for even more innovative and exciting readings of ancient texts. When scholars ... dismiss the film—for example, saying it has the narrative and emotional depth of “an elaborate Fourth of July fireworks display”—they give the opposite impression, that Nolan is careless or ignorant. I worry this kind of response says more about the limitations of academia itself—and what kinds of conversations it considers serious or respectable—than it does about the inadequacies of Nolan’s film. Why, after all, should we care more about what Homer might think of uses of his work than who his poem might speak to now? Who are these texts for if not us? 

articulates incredibly well the limitations of the current level of discussion about The Odyssey and how shallow much of the criticism thrown it's way.  This is not to say that it is a film that can't be criticised, this piece does a fair bit of that itself, but that it deserves to be treated seriously in it's critiques.  

If I have to read another post here that claims to be so much smarter than anyone who liked this film but doesn't even catch Nolan's use of non Odyssey pieces and the subversion of the Sinon character I will lose my goddamn mind.

### Top 4 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. >In saying all this, I don’t mean to suggest that Wilson is wrong about what would make a good adaptation of The Odyssey

But Wilson never attempts to say what would make a good adaptation.  I hate this narrative that Wilson is against any different tellings of the Odyssey, that she views it as her property, that she's being a stuffy academic.  The core of her essay is that Nolan made an uninteresting movie.
  - People unfortunately can't get past the strawman they build up for themselves and can't escape the discourse they've seen online. They just assume it's all the same all the time. I hate the lazy costumes of the film but people will still argue with me about realism even though my argument has nothing to do with that but because it's what they want to believe, it's what they'll argue
  - She literally does when she complains about there being no sex scenes among other things. Like she literally rants about all the things it is missing in her view. Did you even read her article?
    - Yes I’ve read it several times and she says the exact opposite to what you’re saying. You can point out things that were left out of an adaptation without condemning the concept of making changes.

In particular though, her line “the food looks horrible and there’s no sex scenes” is not complaining about something the movie is “missing”. I mean, not something missing from the poem. The poem doesn’t have sex scenes or visual depictions of food. These things are trappings of movies, and she found this movie to be a dull affair and that was in part due to it lacking these things.

Surely you’re not against a movie review saying a movie was missing certain things that made it good, right? That’s kind of the point of a review. And she’s not saying they’re missing from the original text because she praises several adaptations that take liberties and directly states that an adaptation doesn’t need to be exact. 
  - > But Wilson never attempts to say what would make a good adaptation.

When she says something about what makes an adaption bad, and says something about what would make an adaption better, then of course she does. 

> I hate this narrative that Wilson is against any different tellings of the Odyssey, that she views it as her property, that she's being a stuffy academic. The core of her essay is that Nolan made an uninteresting movie.

## 5. A Bittersweet Life - Rewatched it after a few years

**Body:** I loved it way more than the first time I watched it. The symbolism in this movie is really amazing and warrants a multiple watches to truly unravel. Sun-Woo live a bitter and cut-throat life which he balances out by eating sweets and deserts. The movie literally opens with him eating a desert which is subsequently interrupted by his bitter life before he could truly relish it. He goes on to take out his frustration, his anger, his bitterness on the goons. Then to evens it out by dropping a massive sugar cube into his little espresso cup like he is trying to numb the bitterness away cover it with the taste of sugar.

His world is turned upside down when he meets a person who bring a real innocence, a sweetness to his life that he no longer thought was possible for him to have, something he had given up on a long time ago. This is something that is especially shown in the event when he is hearing her performance and is interrupted by Mun-Suk bringing his out of the sweetness into the bitter world. He for the first time lashes out in Mun-Suk's face insults him in front of everyone even though up until now he was putting up with his antics. Being done he rushes to Hee-Soo's side craving the sweetness she brings in her life only to see it being interrupted by her boyfriend.

IMO Hee-Soo to Sun-Woo was more than just a crush she was for him the perfect antidote to his bitterness. He could not come to terms with killing her and taking away the one perfect thing he has found in his bitter world. 

Even moments before his death he calls her not to talk to her just hear her voice one last time to numb the bitterness of his death with her sweet innocent voice. 

The Buddhism parallels with the branches scene during Hee-Soo's performance, the final quote before his death, his evaluating himself in his reflection at multiple points throughout the story all of it is just amazing.

The soundtrack it just majestic. I couldn't find it on Spotify if anybody knows somewhere I can get it please tell me.

The only part of the story that I didn't quite understand was why Kang didn't kill or hurt Hee-Soo after finding out about her affair.
